md: A shared lock caps allocator throughput at $1/c$ no matter how many cores you add. The fix is not a faster lock but keeping the common path on state that only one CPU (or thread) touches, and going to shared state rarely and in batches.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: Promotion: finding hot pages trapped in slow memory
md: Promotion needs two signals: *is this page hot* (recency of access) and *can we afford to move it* (free space, rate limit). Missing either one turns tiering into a migration storm.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: From threads to blocks: the Triton programming model
md: CUDA: *scalar program, blocked threads*. Triton: *blocked program, scalar threads*. In Triton you think about which tile each program owns; the compiler thinks about which thread holds which element.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Everything is a token: Chameleon and Emu3
md: Misconception: "sharing a vocabulary makes images and text equally easy to model." Image tokens have very different entropy from text tokens, and the paper attributes the instability exactly to modalities of different entropy sharing one softmax.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Syscalls become function calls: one address space, one privilege level
md: Unikernel speed comes from **removing the user/kernel crossing**, not from a faster CPU path. Gains are largest for small, syscall-heavy requests and near zero for compute-bound code.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Graph traversal: memory layout, cache misses and prefetching
md: In graph search the expensive part per hop is often the first touch of a random vector, not the arithmetic. Contiguous fixed-size blocks, aligned vectors, prefetching and smaller (compressed) vectors all attack that same miss.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: WorkerGroups, resource pools and DataProto dispatch
md: Do not read `world_size` as the data-parallel size. On 8 GPUs with TP 2 a WorkerGroup has 8 workers but only 4 data shards. Splitting the batch 8 ways would hand different samples to two GPUs that must run the same sharded matmul together.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Merging similar frames: MovieChat and MA-LMM memory banks
md: Merging is lossy and question-blind. It removes what *looks* redundant, so a brief, visually small change (a number on a scoreboard updating) can be averaged away before anyone asks about it. MA-LMM's ablation found accuracy saturating at a memory length around 10 to 20 for 100 input frames on its benchmarks; that says those benchmarks are redundant, not that every question is.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Where ViT-B/16's 86 million parameters live
md: Library checkpoints may differ slightly from this count. Hugging Face's `ViTModel` can include an extra pooler layer (a D x D dense plus tanh); `ViTForImageClassification` builds the backbone without it and reads the raw CLS state. Always check with a parameter count on the actual model rather than trusting a model card.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: Why per-step tokens break at 50 Hz, and how FAST compresses them
md: FAST spends tokens on information, not on time steps. Across datasets from 5 Hz to 50 Hz it produced roughly 30 tokens per arm per 1-second chunk, so the token count tracks the complexity of the motion rather than the control rate.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Token budgets: bits per image, 1D tokenizers and early fusion
md: TiTok's 32 tokens are not an image patch each. Flattening a 2D grid into a sequence still keeps the grid constraint; a 1D tokenizer lets each token describe any part of the image. Ids from different tokenizers are not interchangeable even at the same length.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Turning an image into tokens a language model can read
md: A VLM in the LLaVA style is just a language model whose input sequence contains extra tokens that came from an image. Every visual token costs context length and compute exactly like a text token.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Where VLMs fail and how they are evaluated
md: Treat a VLM as a strong but fallible reader: give it legible pixels, ask for fields it can copy rather than compute, and verify with rules the document itself provides.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Making wait-free fast: fast path, slow path, and when to bother
md: Check every layer. A wait-free algorithm is only as wait-free as its primitives and helpers: a `fetch_or` that compiles to a CAS loop, an allocator that takes a lock, or a reclamation scheme that can block will each reintroduce unbounded waiting.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Why a pool needs more than one shared queue
md: Misconception: more workers always means more throughput. With one locked queue, past the knee extra workers only add waiters on the same lock and the same cache line. The model here is deliberately simple, but the cap of 1/c is real for any serial section.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Cheap scaling studies, continual training and failure modes
md: WSD separates *making progress* (long constant-LR trunk) from *cashing it in* (short cooldown). That separation is what makes checkpoints reusable, runs extendable and scaling studies roughly linear in the number of model sizes instead of quadratic.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: When zero-copy pays: measurements, limits and choices
md: Zero-copy pays when messages are large, the CPU is the bottleneck and the program does not touch the bytes. Any step that reads every byte (software checksums, encryption, hashing, compression) brings the copy back almost for free and erases most of the win.
